To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Miocene porphyry copper deposit formation in the Gangdise belt is related to a two-stage crustal growth process, the first stage is dominated by subduction-related arc magmas and crustal fertilization, and the second stage is dominated by collisional crustal growth and mixing between subduction-modified crust and lithospheric mantle melts.
the Miocene high-K magmatic rocks are characterized by adakitie affinity with high-SY and La/Yb, and high Mg# and evolved Sr-Nd- Hf isotopic compositions.

the lower crust with metallogenic potential was formed in the Paleocene− Eocene, and the metallogenic giant porphyry copper deposit was formed in the Miocene, and the source of the metallo-genic magmas is composed of the Paleocene − Eocene lower crust and the lithospheric mantle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the crustal growth and its relation to metallogeny in a collisional orogen, and the results are expected to provide new insights into the genesis of giant porphyry Cu deposits.
the crustal growth process of collisional orogen, and the origin of porphyry deposits associated with collisional orogenic magmatic rocks.
the spatial and temporal evolution of the crust in the Gangdise belt and the origin of the metallogeny in this region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Miocene porphyry deposits were formed by the partial melting of a Paleocene−Eoocene arc lower crust and the mixing of the lithospheric mantle with a subduction-modification effect, and this process is consistent with the crustal growth model of the continental collisional orogen.

the lower crustal source for the Miocene porphyry deposit-forming magmas is the Paleocene− Eocene arc magmas modified by the subduction process and the mantle source is a mixture of trachytic magma derived from the lithospheric mantle and the Paleocene−Oligocene arc magma.

the Miocene porphyry deposits formed during the collision stage, and the lower crust source was mainly composed of the subduction-related Paleocene−Eoocene arc rocks with input from lithosphere mantle-derived trachyte magmas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the collisional crustal growth is a process that involves the subduction-modified juvenile lower crust and the lithospheric mantle.
the collisional orogenic crustal growth is a process of reworking the pre-existing crustal materials and the lithospheric mantle.
the Miocene porphyry copper mineralization in southern Tibet is related to the partial melting of the Paleocene-Eocene arc crust with input from the lithospheric mantle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the crustal evolution in the collisional setting is different from that in the continental arc setting.
the metallogenic potential of a subduction-related magmatic arc may be enhanced by a subsequent continental collision.
the collisional stage is the key stage for the formation of porphyry deposits, which is different from the subduction stage.
